bib.title: Learning to Rewrite Tool Descriptions for Reliable LLM-Agent Tool Use

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: All 29 pages (95,803 chars) read: main text pp.1-9, appendix text for A (annotator prompt), B (setup, B.1 teacher forcing, B.3 training), C, D, E and Tables 7-11. I skimmed the long prompt listings in A/B (about chars 54.5k-63k and 67.5k-83.9k) and checked them for setup facts only. References skimmed. No instructions embedded in the PDF text.

SOURCE: "Learning to Rewrite Tool Descriptions for Reliable LLM-Agent Tool Use", Ruocheng Guo*, Kaiwen Dong*, Xiang Gao, Kamalika Das; Intuit AI Research, Mountain View. arXiv 2602.20426v2, 29 Apr 2026. Marked "Preprint. Under review." No venue.

CORE CLAIM: Tool descriptions written for human developers cap agent accuracy, and the problem grows with catalog size. The authors fine-tune a small model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct) to rewrite a tool's description from its schema alone ("Trace-Free+"). It is trained by curriculum, with trace-summary inputs first and trace-free inputs later. Targets are descriptions (D2) built from agent failure traces. The rewrite recurs on five patterns: scope, cross-tool dependencies, output, parameter constraints and cross-parameter dependencies.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (setup in each line)
- Scaling: 0-150 extra tools, StableToolBench G2-G3, GPT-4.1, non-teacher-forced, query-level (QL). Degradation vs D0 is reduced by 29.23%. Average QL success is up 60.89% vs D0. The extra candidates are 10% relevant and 90% random; this is read off Fig. 3 with no table.
- Multi-step (G2+G3), GPT-4.1, teacher-forced, StableToolBench 764 solvable queries: QL 44.6 vs D0 33.5 (+11.1) and D1 41.5 (+3.1). The paper quotes only these averages. Its ± values appear to be over repeated runs, but the run count is never stated.
- Single-step G1: Trace-Free+ 60.7 QL vs D1 61.6 vs D0 59.2. D0 is already near the ceiling, and D1 is as good or better.
- RestBench QL: TMDB 74.9 vs D0 49.5 and D1 58.0 (+51.3% relative vs D0); Spotify 49.3 vs D0 34.9 (+41.3% relative). Models were trained only on StableToolBench tools.
- Agent fine-tuning (Qwen3-4B agent, QL): StableToolBench 37.4 (base+D0), 40.0 (fine-tuned+D0), 40.1 (base+TF+), 41.8 (fine-tuned+TF+). RestBench 54.1, 55.0, 62.1, 62.9.
- BFCLv2 (Table 11): GPT-4.1 Live 79.28 to 80.63; Claude Sonnet 4.5 Live 52.40 to 53.45; Gemini-3-pro-preview Live 84.98 to 86.41. Non-Live gains are 0.3-2.4 points.
- Cost: the paper reports no cost figures. Hardware was 8xA100 for training, and GPT-4.1 (2025-05-14) was the agent.

ABLATIONS
- Curriculum vs trace-free-only training: G2+G3 QL 44.6 vs 44.1 (Table 1); TMDB QL 74.9 vs 57.7 (Table 2).
- Trace-free share per stage (Table 10): the two-stage (0.1, 0.9) split was best; three stages did worse.
- Pattern coverage on Media and Finance tools (Table 8). D0 → TF+: scope 3.3% → 97.2%; parameter constraints 9.9% → 94.2%; cross-parameter 0.3% → 17.1%; output description 11.6% → 27.0%. D1 gets 99.7% on scope and 98.6% on output.
- EasyTool scores below D0 (G2+G3 and G1).

QUOTES
- p.1: "Tool descriptions are often written for human developers and tolerate ambiguity that agents cannot resolve, particularly as the number of candidate tools grows."
- p.1: a tool "Fetches the year a particular scientific work was published" led the agent to pass "Law of Universal Gravitation" as work_title; saying "full title" fixed it.
- p.7: "From 0–150 additional tools, Trace-Free+ reduces performance degradation of D0 by 29.23% and improves over D0 by 60.89% on average."
- p.4: the Walk Score example. D0 said only "Get Walk Score", with a format field copied from a movie API. The rewrite added that lat is in [-90, 90], that bike and transit must be exactly '1', and "Do not use for real-time traffic data or historical trends."

LIMITS
- The authors concede three things. The generator is only Qwen3-4B-Instruct (p.9). Trace-Free+ does not beat D1 on single-step queries, and "D0 is already near the ceiling." The model "may occasionally hallucinate constraints", such as value ranges the server does not enforce; this is not measured (p.9).
- Not shown:
  - The scaling gains are read off a figure, with no table.
  - The run count is not given.
  - The candidate pad is 90% random APIs, so selection is easy by design.
  - The test is REST APIs from RapidAPI, TMDB and Spotify. There is no MCP, code or database evidence.
  - Gains are measured with GPT-4.1 on the main benchmarks, and with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini-3-pro-preview only on BFCLv2.
  - Teacher forcing hides selection errors that would compound in real use.
  - No human study of description quality.
  - The ground-truth tool labels came from GPT-4.1, with 96 of 100 spot-checked correct.
  - The D1 comparison is at its strongest on multi-step queries.
  - The learned-rewriter method is not needed to get most of the lift: D1, a prompted template, already gets most of the gain on short tasks.

BUILDS ON: Hsieh et al. 2023 (Tool documentation enables zero-shot tool-usage, arXiv); Qu et al. 2024 (DRAFT, as the paper cites it for task decomposition and degradation with candidate size) and Qu et al. 2025 (DRAFT, the paper's per-tool trace-based revision baseline); Fang et al. 2025 (Play2Prompt, arXiv); Yuan et al. 2025 (EasyTool); Gao et al. 2025 (RIMRULE, arXiv 2601.00086, used to extract rules from failure traces); Bengio et al. 2009 (curriculum learning, ICML); Guo et al. 2024 (StableToolBench, ACL Findings); Qin et al. 2023 (ToolBench/ToolLLM); Song et al. 2023 (RestBench); Patil et al. 2025 (BFCL); Parnas 1972 (information hiding, as the stated principle).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig. 1 (p.3) shows the D0 vs rewritten description and the resulting correct call. Table 9 (p.28) gives the Walk Score, Trackmania and League of Legends before/after descriptions. Fig. 3 (p.8, scaling curves) is the one for the "tool discovery at scale" claim.

FIT TO 03-tool-design.md
- Best fit: "ACI, not API". The description is the main lever, and a bad description sinks a capable agent. D0 to D1 alone moves multi-step QL from 33.5 to 41.5.
- Second: "Schema rules" / "The five-section tool contract". The five pattern categories (Table 7) and Table 9 are a usable checklist: scope and when NOT to use, upstream dependency, output fields, parameter constraints, paired or exclusive parameters.
- Weaker: "Tool discovery at scale". Fig. 3 supports description quality under 150+ candidates, but the 90% random pad makes it a soft test.
- Poor fit for "The clarity test": there is no human clarity test.
- Overall: moderately relevant but not strong. The learned-rewriter method itself is off-topic for a course on writing tool descriptions. Cite the diagnostic and the five patterns only.
